summary: A 1976 note on the syntax used to specify addresses in network mail. It looks at how addresses can be written so that mail systems on different hosts can understand them.

eli5.summary: Letters need a clear address on the envelope. This note talks about how to write email addresses so every computer can read them.

questions: how were mailing lists handled in 1976
subtitle: A richer syntax for specifying email addresses and mailing lists.

tldr.problem: RFC 680's mail syntax conflated a person's name with their address, could not easily handle mailing lists that should be carried in messages, and offered no way to send mail to secondary mailboxes.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 720 proposes a syntax that separately specifies a person's name, their user ID (login name), an optional secondary mailbox or file, and the host. Mailing lists can be given a group name and either expanded inline or referenced by pathname.
tldr.outcome: The proposal was a stepping stone toward more complete email addressing. Modern email standards use variations of this approach, with clear separation between display names and mailbox specifications.

today: RFC 720 was a proposal that informed later email standards. Modern email addresses follow similar principles of separating display names (RFC 5322) from network addresses, though the specific syntax evolved differently as SMTP became the standard.

sections.title: Email Addressing Problems
sections.content: RFC 720 identifies four limitations of the existing RFC 680 mail syntax. First, people's names and their computer addresses are not the same thing but the syntax did not distinguish them. Second, mailing lists could become longer than the messages they carried, and there was no good way to include expanded lists in messages. Third, mail systems often needed to include the full list of recipients in messages to enable replies to all members. Finally, the syntax provided no way to direct mail to secondary mailboxes or files beyond a user's primary inbox.
sections.eli5: Email systems needed better ways to show names, handle big lists, and send mail to different places.

sections.title: The New Address Format
sections.content: The proposed syntax separates four components: a person's name, their user ID (online directory name or login), an optional secondary mailbox, and the host machine. For mailing lists, a group name precedes the member list. Lists can be either expanded inline in the address field or referenced by a file pathname. The syntax uses parentheses, brackets, braces or angle brackets for nesting, with quotation marks allowed for names containing ambiguous characters like spaces.
sections.eli5: Instead of squishing everything together, the new format lets you write a human name separately from the computer address.

sections.title: Examples and Formal Definition
sections.content: The RFC provides examples ranging from simple addresses like "Walker at ISI" to complex mailing lists with personal names like "Steve Walker"[Walker at ISI]. Teleconferencing addresses can direct messages to special mailboxes per conversation. A formal BNF specification defines the complete syntax, replacing and simplifying the complex field definitions in RFC 680. The syntax is designed for inter-system communication; user-facing interfaces could use simpler representations.
sections.eli5: The format is described in a way computers can parse precisely, so mail systems from different companies can all understand each other.

references.text: Crocker, D., "Format of network messages", RFC 680, April 1975.
